🚨The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group, with the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), are headed to the Middle East, two U.S. officials told Fox News.

The ships are expected to arrive by the end of November, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region. Fox News reports about 6,000 are in the carrier strike group and about 4,200 in the MEU and Makin Island group.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt would be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. The USS Makin Island would be the second amphibious assault ship with an embarked MEU in the region, alongside USS Boxer and the 11th MEU. 

The deployment comes as President Trump has said renewed military action against Iran remains possible after the November 3 midterm elections.

lha-7.t: How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sa…
lha-7.tx:
How many Americans know that after two U.S. Navy warships were blown open by sea mines in the Persian Gulf in 1991, five hundred and eleven Japanese sailors sailed wooden boats straight into the deadliest minefield on earth to clear the way for the American fleet?

In February 1991, Iraqi mines tore holes in the amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton. Over one thousand mines still choked the waters off Kuwait.

Western television commentators mocked Japan for only sending money during the war. Those commentators stopped laughing when Captain Taosa Ochiai and six Japanese naval vessels steamed eight thousand miles into the blazing summer heat of the Persian Gulf.

Why did Japan send four tiny wooden-hulled minesweepers, Hikoshima, Yurishima, Awashima, and Sakushima, instead of steel destroyers? Because Iraq had planted Italian-made Manta bottom mines on the seafloor that detonated the instant they sensed the magnetic field or engine hum of a steel hull.

Only non-magnetic hulls built of timber could float over them without blowing up.

Working in 120-degree heat alongside the U.S. Navy, Japanese minesweepers took on the most dangerous shallow sectors where sunken oil tankers and deadly Manta mines waited.

When sonar spotted a mine on the bottom that mechanical cables could not cut, Japanese explosive ordnance divers strapped on flippers, swam down into the murky water by hand, and placed explosive charges right next to live warheads.

Across ninety-nine straight days under the desert sun, Japan's wooden boats destroyed thirty-four deadly mines without losing a single sailor.

On their final day in the Gulf, U.S. Navy commanders stood at attention and saluted the sunburned Japanese crews who had cleared the sea in silence.

Real allies do not boast on television. They take the deadliest sector and clear the path for their friends.

cvn-73.t: 🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Inside the carrier keeping the world's oil moving: US jets fly into Hormuz every night to shoot down Iranian missiles aimed at tankers What the Wall Stre…
cvn-73.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Inside the carrier keeping the world's oil moving: US jets fly into Hormuz every night to shoot down Iranian missiles aimed at tankers

What the Wall Street Journal saw aboard the USS George Washington:

• F-35Cs and F/A-18s launch nightly with electronic-warfare jets, radar planes and sub-hunting helicopters to build an umbrella over tankers in a strait just 20 miles wide

• More than 3,000 commercial ships escorted through in six months, Gulf oil exports now above prewar levels, and CENTCOM marking 1.5 billion barrels shipped since summer

• The US says 95% of traffic passes safely and pilots report a 100% intercept rate when they're on station with missiles, though Iran sometimes fires at more ships than they can cover

• October was the most violent month for shipping since the war began, with more than 35 incidents logged by UKMTO

• 50,000 US troops and 20 Navy ships in the region, carriers setting modern records for days at sea without a port call, destroyer tours extended again

• The Navy's top admiral says sailors "need a port call" and is setting up a repair hub on Diego Garcia

• Washington's efforts to build an international coalition to share the job have gone nowhere

The mission is working, and that's the best argument against a strike: oil is flowing, Iran's economy is collapsing, so hold the line indefinitely.

The catch is the people doing the holding.

Every month adds $2 to $3 billion, more worn-out jets and longer stretches away from home for crews who were promised relief, and the White House now has to decide whether the next week brings a short, intense campaign or tells those sailors the blockade is their job for the foreseeable future.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

cvn-68.t: 🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor? The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise…
cvn-68.tx:
🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor?

The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise into one of aviation cinema’s most memorable encounters: two F-14 Tomcats facing Japanese Zero fighters.

Transported back to December 1941, USS Nimitz carries enough firepower to change the course of the Pacific War. Captain Matthew Yelland, played by Kirk Douglas, faces a question no commander’s training could prepare him for: should he intervene?

Then comes the order: “Splash the Zeros.”

Six years before Top Gun, the Tomcat was already a movie star. Real Navy aircrews from VF-84 (the Jolly Rogers) flew the F-14s, while modified T-6 Texans portrayed the Japanese fighters.

Behind the fantasy was demanding aerial choreography: fast jets, much slower propeller aircraft, and camera crews trying to capture both in the same frame. A B-25 camera aircraft eventually helped make the aerial choreography work.

The scene delivers the spectacle. The premise leaves you with the question.

If you commanded USS Nimitz (CVN-68), would you change history?

Follow @Vanguard_WW2 for military history and the stories behind its most memorable screen moments.

al-dhafra.t: 🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipm…
al-dhafra.tx:
🇮🇷⚔️🪖🇺🇸🇧🇭‼️The American Base Targeted 159 Times by Iran

The Al Dhafra air base in the UAE, hosting a range of reconnaissance, communication, and support equipment, is a key node in the network of US and allied air operations in the Persian Gulf. This base was targeted 159 times during the Iran-Iraq War (Ramadan War).

The equipment stationed at this base connected reconnaissance, information transmission, command, and air operation support elements; a system that can be described as the "eyes, brain, and arm of air operations."

Information from the base's radars and reconnaissance aircraft was combined to create a common picture of the regional situation, which was then provided to the Al Udeid air operations center. Communication centers and satellite data reception facilities also served as a link for transmitting this information to commanders and operational units.

In the operational section, the 380th Air Expeditionary Wing managed missions related to reconnaissance aircraft, fighter jets, tankers, and air support. Large fuel storage tanks and aircraft maintenance facilities also provided the necessary support for the continuity of these missions.

The presence of US, UAE, and French forces gave Al Dhafra a multinational status, making it one of the key points for connecting the air power of these countries in the region.

The diversity of these targets indicates that in the attacks, in addition to aircraft, the necessary infrastructure for detection, reconnaissance, data transmission, command, and the continuation of operations was also a target. However, the targeting of each of these facilities, in itself, does not necessarily indicate the extent of the damage or its removal from the operational cycle.

The operational consequence highlighted in this account is the transformation of Al Dhafra from a support base into a point vulnerable to repeated attacks. This situation forces the US to allocate part of its capabilities and resources to protecting the base, dispersing equipment, and maintaining communication between the components of the network.

Farsna

muwaffaq-salti.t: 🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Iran hit 274 buildings on 24 US bases in six months and aimed for the barracks where troops sleep, and the Pentagon still won't say what it cost What the…
muwaffaq-salti.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 Iran hit 274 buildings on 24 US bases in six months and aimed for the barracks where troops sleep, and the Pentagon still won't say what it cost

What the Wall Street Journal found in tens of thousands of satellite images:

-274 damaged structures at 24 installations across Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iraq in the war's first six months

-119 buildings hit in the first two weeks alone, most of them in Kuwait; the Fifth Fleet's base in Bahrain was largely evacuated

-After the ceasefire collapsed in July, Iran shifted fire west to Jordan and hit buildings half the size of its earlier targets, matching housing units; the July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti killed 3 Americans and damaged 19 barracks

-Iranian media claims of strikes on troop housing doubled in that stretch; the Journal found damage to housing at three more bases the same week

-More than 20 US service members dead and 400-plus wounded before the Pentagon stopped publishing war-specific casualty figures in July

-Base damage priced at a minimum of $5 billion and possibly $15 billion, on top of the $47.1 billion war bill; CSIS puts rebuilding alone above $4 billion

-Hegseth declared Iran's missile program "functionally defeated" on March 13 and Trump said its missiles were "just about used up" on April 1; Iran kept hitting bases for five more months

-Sen. Murphy was barred from visiting Al Udeid, where at least a dozen buildings show damage, and says the Pentagon is "withholding information" to hide the war's cost

Hegseth's story and the satellite record don't match, and the gap is the problem for next week. 

The Pentagon moved troops off bases and is now talking about pulling back from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia entirely, which is what you do when you expect the next round to hit harder, and officials admit Iran has saved its best missiles.

Source: Wall Street Journal / Writer: Daniel

muwaffaq-salti.t: A major @WSJ investigation documents the extensive damage Iranian missile and drone attacks have inflicted on US military bases across the Middle East, and how…
muwaffaq-salti.tx:
A major @WSJ investigation documents the extensive damage Iranian missile and drone attacks have inflicted on US military bases across the Middle East, and how Iran's targeting has evolved over the course of the war.

The Pentagon privately estimates at least $5 billion in damage to US bases, potentially as much as $15 billion. That's on top of $47.1 billion in other war costs through October 16. More than 20 US servicemembers have been killed in war-related activity, with over 400 wounded before the July ceasefire collapsed, when the Pentagon stopped publishing war-specific casualty figures.

In the first two weeks alone, at least 119 buildings across 13 installations were damaged, particularly in Kuwait. Iran also struck radar, missile-defense, and communications infrastructure. The US largely evacuated several bases, including its Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and major installations in Kuwait.

Perhaps most significant is how Iranian attacks evolved. Following the July ceasefire collapse, Iran increasingly struck bases farther from its borders, particularly in Jordan, while hitting smaller, more specific targets, including buildings housing American troops. A July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan killed three US servicemembers and damaged at least 19 buildings where troops sleep.

The WSJ's satellite analysis suggests growing Iranian targeting precision and an ability to adapt its operations despite months of US and Israeli strikes. The Pentagon has been forced to disperse personnel, reconsider its regional basing posture, and weigh relocating installations farther from Iran.

All of this stands in striking contrast to repeated public claims by Trump administration officials that Iran's missile capabilities had been effectively destroyed. In March, Hegseth declared Iran's ballistic missile production capacity functionally defeated. In April, Trump said its missiles were nearly exhausted. In July, days after the deadly Jordan strike, Hegseth described Iran as "completely overmatched and crushed" and "combat ineffective."

Yet Iran continued striking US installations, inflicting casualties and billions in damage.

The broader strategic implication is that degrading Iran's military capabilities has not eliminated its ability to impose substantial costs on the US regional military presence.

The war has exposed the vulnerability of America's large, fixed bases to Iranian missiles and drones, raising difficult questions for the US about the sustainability of its posture in the Middle East and the consequences of another round of escalation.

🔴The Islamic Republic deliberately targeted sleeping American soldiers rather than focusing on military hardware like ships or missile interceptors.

The Wall Street Journal analyzed tens of thousands of satellite images, identifying 274 damaged structures across 24 U.S. military sites in the first six months of the war, most of which were living quarters for American personnel.

I wrote about Iran's shift to counter-personnel targeting to deter attacks on Iranian civilians in July. On the 25th, based on vulnerability theory, I predicted that Iran will retaliate in this manner to the US attacks then underway. (

On the 26th, we got confirmation of both counter-personnel strikes and the establishment of the new deterrence equation. ( Since then the US has not stuck Iranian civilian sites.

The Journal's recent report allows us to further 'process trace' the posited deterrence equation. (

'Within days of the deadly July 17 strike at Muwaffaq Salti, the Journal found damage at three other installations to buildings that current and former U.S. servicemembers said resembled base housing. That same week, U.S. officials privately expressed worry about Iran targeting troops where they sleep.

Iran was also hitting smaller buildings, one sign of the precision that has increasingly alarmed U.S. officials. Structures damaged after the ceasefire collapsed were less than half of the size of the ones hit earlier, the Journal found. Base housing—often converted shipping containers or even tents—tends to be small, some of the current and former servicemembers said.

Iran’s own public statements reflected this shift. From July 7 to Aug. 28, Iran claimed more than 40 strikes on U.S. installations, according to a Journal analysis of four Iranian state-affiliated media outlets. More than three-quarters of those claims described specific types of buildings at named installations, compared with less than half earlier in the war—and claims of strikes targeting housing doubled.'

The scribes rolled out one AEI 'expert' to say, “There’s definitely been an effort by the Iranians to inflict casualties on U.S. forces." No shit, Sherlock. The observation might even have been interesting in September. You guys are so far behind the curve, it is painful to watch.

Another blobhead is rolled out to say, “The type and number of strikes over time also contains signals about [Iranian] magazine depth.” Sure. But the signal-to-noise ratio is very poor.

The problem is that this information is completely masked by strategic husbanding of the arsenal. One cannot tell whether strike tempo is lower because the they are running low or because they are choosing to hold their weapons in reserve.

The decisive issue is the rate of production of Iranian theater weapons. There is reason to believe that their rate of production is higher than it has ever been. For one, they have transferred at least 2000 to the Houthis. For another, they are test firing dozens. Tehran understands very well that the missile inventory is a matter of life and death for the state.

Iran's strategic patience, their manifest willingness to drag out the war, to hold back on escalation, may have less to do with dwindling inventories and more to do with their assessment that the war will last a long time no matter what strategy they pursue. No signal on magazine depth is therefore recoverable at this point.

If and when they fail to retaliate when clear red lines are crossed, we may have reason to suspect that dwindling inventories are responsible. We just haven't seen that yet. Nor should we expect to see it any time soon.

The US has probably been disarmed more than Iran. This conclusion is even stronger once we think in rates of production rather than inventory levels, as is appropriate for a protracted war.

incirlik.t: A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️ 3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sl…
incirlik.tx:
A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️

3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sleep. You’re going somewhere else, carrying something different, and you’ll do it again tomorrow. Move the mission. 

There I am, coffee in one hand, flight bag in the other, eyes still half-glued shut, shuffling out to our big beautiful C-141 or C-17 beast under those harsh ramp lights. The “bag drag.”

The air’s crisp, the jet’s APU or power cart are already humming that low, throaty growl, as the jet wakes up for a global joyride. When it starts up, it barks at you. But that’s a good sign. And, the bittersweet smell of diesel exhaust and jet fumes. You grow to love it. I can’t explain it. It always felt like “home” no matter where in the world we were. 

Crew piles in: loadmasters cracking jokes, engineers double-checking the flyability of this metal marvel, and me sliding into the left seat thinking, “Alright, Lord, let’s do this again.”

It’s inherent. Not a lot of creative thought required. The crew, like a group of ants taking orders from the queen, automatically dives into their respective duties and checklists like clockwork. No direction needed here. It’s symbiosis. 

We crank the engines, taxi out into the dark, ramp lights fading into a world of blue and white lights, suck down some awful coffee, tell a few jokes, and blast off as the sun’s still thinking about showing up. 

The possibilities were endless. Could be one hop to Ramstein for fuel and some bratwurst, next leg to Incirlik where the pita bread’s fresh, the hookah’s are smoking, and the tension’s thicker than the Turkish coffee. Buy your pistachios here. 

Then it’s “wheels up” again. Maybe Diego Garcia for a quick dip in that insane blue water and warm beer, or over to Yokota where the ramen and beer hits different at 0200 local. And where I met my wife. 

Skipping across continents like stones on a pond, chasing daylight, dodging weather, and hauling everything from the SEALS, to the 82nd Airborne, to nuclear weapons, to Thanksgiving turkeys. Hell, once I flew a single generator to Nouadhibou, Mauritania. 

And a bunch of liquor to American embassies throughout the world. 

You land in one country for thirty minutes, grab a weird local snack that’ll haunt your stomach for days, chat with the ground crew in broken English and hand signals, sign some funky foreign forms pretending to know what they were, then you’re back in the air chasing the next sunrise. 

Jet lag? What jet lag. This is the life: stars above, stars on the flag on your sleeve, and the pure rush of knowing you’re part of the greatest airlift machine the world has ever seen. And we mattered, bigly. My country gave me a heavy jet and said “fly here.” It still blows my mind.

akrotiri.t: UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll —— According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Min…
akrotiri.tx:
UK expands military backing for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen despite rising civilian death toll
——
According to an investigation by Declassified UK, Britain’s Ministry of Defense (MoD) has expanded its military assistance to Saudi Arabia, deploying Royal Air Force (RAF) Typhoon fighter jets and providing critical aerial refueling for Saudi airstrikes targeting Yemen.

The increased support was authorized by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, who previously advocated for an arms embargo against Riyadh over its civilian casualty record in Yemen, but is now presiding over direct British involvement as Saudi strikes hit civilian centers.

Data from the Yemen Data Project reveals that Saudi airstrikes caused more civilian casualties last month than in any single period since 2022, resulting in at least 66 deaths and 90 injuries—including eight children.

Among the deadliest incidents was a September 22 strike on a residential home in Mokha that killed six civilians, followed days later by an attack on a market in the Al-Taiziyah district of Taiz that killed seven and injured 40 others.

Despite the rising toll, London agreed to send up to 20 Voyager aerial refueling sorties from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus with their transponders deactivated, while deploying Typhoons from Qatar to support Saudi air operations without charging the kingdom for the military assistance.

The escalation follows the collapse of a four-year UN-brokered ceasefire in July, triggered when Saudi-led forces bombed Sanaa International Airport. In response to the breakdown, Yemen's Armed Forces have launched retaliatory drone and missile strikes against strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

While ten leading British trade unions and human rights monitors have demanded an immediate halt to UK military collaboration, British officials maintain that RAF deployments serve strictly "defensive counter air" purposes to protect regional allies.

The U.S. is now at a 3rd fork in the road, and POTUS either has to, or already has decided which direction to take.

He explains what the training is for:

“If combat is so intense, large scale combat operations or high intensity conflict to where there is no time to recover your dead, so you bury them where they are.”

Aguilar says US bases already know how to run 90 days on their own, so the Pentagon announcing it is a message to Tehran, not a new capability.

Add the rushed order of battlefield ketamine wafers and the air defense launchers he says went up at Mar-a-Lago, and he reads it as a crew pulling on life jackets while telling passengers nothing’s wrong.

If he’s right, the plan Trump has signed off on assumes American casualties at a scale this country hasn’t seen in 70 years, and nobody in Washington has told the public that.

pearl-harbor.t: The worst battleship of WW2 might be Japan's Fuso. A ship so badly designed that its own navy kept it out of the fight for almost the entire war, and then sent…
pearl-harbor.tx:
The worst battleship of WW2 might be Japan's Fuso. A ship so badly designed that its own navy kept it out of the fight for almost the entire war, and then sent it to die in the last battleship duel in history.

When Fuso was completed in 1915, she was briefly one of the most powerful battleships in the world. Twelve 14-inch guns. Japan's first true super-dreadnought.

But the designers made a fatal choice. They spread those twelve guns across six turrets, running almost the whole length of the ship. Two at the front, two in the middle, two at the back.

That meant six separate ammunition magazines scattered along the hull. Huge stretches of the ship had to be armored to protect explosives. The armor couldn't cover all of it well. And when the middle turrets fired, the blast interfered with the rest of the ship.

Then in the 1930s, Japan modernized her. They gave her new engines, more armor, and a towering "pagoda" mast. It rose so high above the deck it looked like it might tip her over. It became one of the strangest silhouettes of any warship ever built.

By WW2, Fuso was old, slow, and fragile. The Japanese Navy knew it.

So when the war started, she mostly sat in home waters. She trained crews. She escorted. She waited. During the biggest naval battles of 1942 and 1943, she barely saw action. Japan even considered cutting off her rear turrets and turning her into a half-carrier, then dropped the idea.

Then came October 1944. Leyte Gulf.

Japan was throwing everything it had at the American landings in the Philippines. Fuso and her near-sister Yamashiro were assigned to Admiral Shoji Nishimura's Southern Force. Their job was to push through Surigao Strait at night and hit the landing beaches.

The Americans were waiting.

At the far end of the strait sat six US battleships, plus cruisers, destroyers, and torpedo boats. Five of those six battleships had been at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Some had been sunk in the mud that day, raised, and rebuilt.

They had come back for revenge.

Early on October 25, 1944, American destroyers charged down the strait in the dark and fired torpedoes. At least one slammed into Fuso around 3 a.m. Fires spread. She fell out of line.

For decades, the story was that Fuso blew up and broke in two, with both burning halves drifting in the strait while the battle raged around them. It's in countless books.

But when her wreck was finally found and surveyed in 2017, it raised real doubts about that story. The truth of her last minutes is still being argued.

What isn't in doubt is how it ended. Fuso went down with nearly her entire crew. Over 1,500 men. Only a handful are believed to have survived.

Minutes later, Yamashiro steamed straight into the American battle line. The US battleships crossed her T and opened fire. Yamashiro was torn apart and sank with Admiral Nishimura aboard.

It was the last time in history that battleships fought battleships.

Fuso spent almost the whole war being kept away from combat because her navy knew what she was. When they finally sent her in, she didn't survive the night.

pearl-harbor.t: If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty…
pearl-harbor.tx:
If you ask any U.S. Navy captain in the Seventh Fleet why America's most powerful warships never want to leave Yokosuka, Japan, they will not point to a treaty. They will point to two thousand Japanese master craftsmen in hard hats waiting inside a 150-year-old stone dry dock.

Keeping the U.S. Seventh Fleet ready to deter conflict across the Indo-Pacific requires constant, grueling hull and combat-system repairs.

Why does the United States Navy not simply sail its damaged or aging warships back to Pearl Harbor or San Diego for maintenance? Because steaming five thousand miles back across the Pacific pulls a frontline warship off patrol for months when every day counts.

Inside Fleet Activities Yokosuka sits Dry Dock Number 1, built out of hand-cut granite stone blocks by Japanese stonemasons in 1871. More than a century and a half later, those ancient stone walls still hold the weight of billion-dollar American Aegis destroyers without cracking an inch.

Working inside those six dry docks is the U.S. Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Center, powered by over two thousand Japanese master welders, pipefitters, shipwrights, and electrical engineers.

Many of these Japanese artisans are second- and third-generation craftsmen whose fathers and grandfathers repaired American warships in the exact same docks.

When the U.S. Seventh Fleet flagship USS Blue Ridge, the oldest operational warship in the U.S. Navy, or an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer comes in from rough seas, Japanese shipwrights and American sailors climb under the massive steel hull shoulder to shoulder.

Through freezing winter nights and sweltering summers, Japanese welders lay down flawless steel seams that U.S. Navy inspectors call the gold standard of the Pacific.

Warships are made of steel. Alliances are kept afloat by the men with welding torches in the bottom of the dock.

pearl-harbor.t: Captain William Callaghan walked onto the scorched teak deck of the U.S. battleship USS Missouri off Okinawa and silenced his angry crew. On April 11, 1945, a…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Captain William Callaghan walked onto the scorched teak deck of the U.S. battleship USS Missouri off Okinawa and silenced his angry crew.

On April 11, 1945, a nineteen-year-old Japanese pilot named Setsuo Ishino slammed his Zero fighter into the starboard side of the 100-million-dollar warship.

The impact tore the plane in half and threw the young pilot's broken body onto the deck. Furious American sailors moved in to wash his remains overboard with fire hoses.

Nobody on that ship had more reason to hate Japan than Captain Callaghan. Just three years earlier off Guadalcanal, Japanese naval gunfire had killed his own brother, Rear Admiral Daniel Callaghan.

Yet Callaghan stepped in front of the body and stopped his men cold.

He ordered his sailors to gather red and white cloth from the ship's signal lockers and sew a Japanese Rising Sun flag by hand overnight.

Some asked why an American captain would waste cloth and honors on a kamikaze pilot during an eighty-two-day battle. Callaghan told his officers that the young man had done his duty to the very end, and in the U.S. Navy, a dead warrior is no longer an enemy.

The next morning, wrapped in canvas beneath that hand-sewn Japanese flag, the nineteen-year-old pilot received a full U.S. Marine rifle salute and Taps before sliding into the Pacific.

Decades later, Japanese townspeople from Chiran came to Pearl Harbor to bow on the deck of the Missouri.

Any nation can hate in the middle of a war. Only a great civilization remembers its honor when the deck is still burning.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane. She was just 22. If you’ve seen Tora! Tor…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane.

She was just 22.

If you’ve seen Tora! Tora! Tora! (1970), you may remember the civilian flight instructor suddenly surrounded by Japanese aircraft.

Her name was Cornelia Fort, a strikingly beautiful young woman and a skilled pilot. The woman behind that scene was real.

On December 7, 1941, Cornelia was giving a flying lesson over Oahu when a Japanese Zero came dangerously close. She seized the controls and narrowly avoided a collision.

Then she saw smoke rising over Pearl Harbor.

Cornelia brought her student safely back to the airfield. She had become one of the few American pilots to witness the opening attack from the air.

In September 1942, she joined the Women’s Auxiliary Ferrying Squadron, becoming one of the pioneering women entrusted with flying military aircraft across the United States. They served as civilians, delivering planes needed for the war effort.

On March 21, 1943, another aircraft struck the BT-13 she was ferrying over Texas. Fort’s aircraft crashed, killing her. She became the first American woman pilot to die in the line of duty flying for the U.S. military.

She was 24.

Hollywood preserved a moment of her life. Her name deserves to be remembered, too.

Follow @Vanguard_WW2 for more overlooked stories of World War II.

See the first post for real photos of Cornelia.

pearl-harbor.t: Five weeks before Pearl Harbor, an American destroyer was blown in half in the North Atlantic. 115 men died. The United States wasn't at war yet. USS Reuben Ja…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Five weeks before Pearl Harbor, an American destroyer was blown in half in the North Atlantic. 115 men died. The United States wasn't at war yet.

USS Reuben James was an old ship by 1941. She was one of the hundreds of narrow, four-funneled "flush deck" destroyers built just after World War I, launched in 1919. She spent the 1920s and 30s patrolling the Mediterranean, the Caribbean and the Atlantic.

Her name came from the early days of the Navy. According to tradition, Reuben James was a boatswain's mate who threw himself in front of a sword blow meant for Stephen Decatur during hand-to-hand fighting at Tripoli in 1804.

By 1941, Britain was fighting Germany alone, and its lifeline was the convoys crossing the Atlantic. The U-boats were strangling them.

President Roosevelt was determined to help without officially going to war. America sent weapons through Lend-Lease. Then American warships began escorting convoys across the western half of the Atlantic, handing them off to the British near Iceland.

It was a war in everything but name.

In September 1941, a U-boat fired at the destroyer USS Greer. Roosevelt ordered American ships to shoot U-boats on sight. On Oct 17, a torpedo hit USS Kearny, killing 11 sailors.

Reuben James was based in Iceland. On Oct 23, she left Newfoundland with four other American destroyers to escort convoy HX-156, a long line of merchant ships bound for Britain.

Before dawn on Oct 31, the convoy was southwest of Iceland. A wolf pack was in the area. Reuben James moved into position between one of the convoy's ammunition ships and where the U-boats were believed to be.

Watching from U-552 was Erich Topp, one of Germany's best U-boat commanders. In the half-light he saw a destroyer and fired two torpedoes.

At least one hit Reuben James on the port side, near the bow.

It set off her forward magazine. The explosion tore the entire front third of the ship away. It sank instantly, taking almost everyone in it, including every officer aboard.

The stern stayed afloat for about five minutes. Survivors scrambled into the freezing water, which was covered in thick fuel oil.

Then the stern sank. As it went down, some of the depth charges on her deck exploded among the men swimming nearby.

The destroyers Niblack and Hilary P. Jones raced in and pulled survivors from the oily sea. Many were so coated in fuel that rescuers could barely hold onto them.

44 enlisted men survived. 115 died, including her captain, Lieutenant Commander Heywood Edwards.

Reuben James was the first American warship sunk in World War II.

The country was shocked and angry. Within weeks, Congress changed the neutrality laws to let American merchant ships carry guns and sail into war zones.

Folk singer Woody Guthrie wrote a song about her, asking listeners to remember the names of the men who went down. It's still sung today.

But America still didn't declare war. That decision was made for it five weeks later, on Dec 7, 1941, at Pearl Harbor.

Erich Topp survived the war. He sank more than 30 ships and became one of Germany's most decorated U-boat commanders. After the war, he joined the new West German Navy and rose to admiral in NATO, serving alongside the navy he had once fought.

Reuben James and her crew are mostly forgotten now, overshadowed by what came after. But for those 115 men, the war started early.

pearl-harbor.t: On December 7, 1941, a 17 year old Japanese American watched Japanese planes attack Pearl Harbor. He rushed to help the wounded. When he tried to join the US A…
pearl-harbor.tx:
On December 7, 1941, a 17 year old Japanese American watched Japanese planes attack Pearl Harbor. He rushed to help the wounded.

When he tried to join the US Army, he was initially rejected because of his ancestry.

Four years later, fighting the Nazis in Italy, a German grenade nearly tore off his right arm.

His shattered hand was still gripping a live grenade. He pulled it free with his left hand, threw it at the Germans, and kept fighting.

He would eventually become one of America's most powerful senators.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor? The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸🇯🇵 What if a modern U.S. aircraft carrier had arrived off Hawaii the day before Pearl Harbor?

The Final Countdown (1980) turns that alternate history premise into one of aviation cinema’s most memorable encounters: two F-14 Tomcats facing Japanese Zero fighters.

Transported back to December 1941, USS Nimitz carries enough firepower to change the course of the Pacific War. Captain Matthew Yelland, played by Kirk Douglas, faces a question no commander’s training could prepare him for: should he intervene?

Then comes the order: “Splash the Zeros.”

Six years before Top Gun, the Tomcat was already a movie star. Real Navy aircrews from VF-84 (the Jolly Rogers) flew the F-14s, while modified T-6 Texans portrayed the Japanese fighters.

Behind the fantasy was demanding aerial choreography: fast jets, much slower propeller aircraft, and camera crews trying to capture both in the same frame. A B-25 camera aircraft eventually helped make the aerial choreography work.

The scene delivers the spectacle. The premise leaves you with the question.

If you commanded USS Nimitz (CVN-68), would you change history?

yokosuka.t: When a young American sailor aboard the nuclear cruiser USS California was dying of a bursting appendix far out in the Pacific Ocean, he was hundreds of miles…
yokosuka.tx:
When a young American sailor aboard the nuclear cruiser USS California was dying of a bursting appendix far out in the Pacific Ocean, he was hundreds of miles beyond the reach of any U.S. Navy helicopter.

Fire Controlman Third Class David Henderson needed surgery fast. A ruptured appendix in rough ocean swells can kill a young sailor long before a warship can steam back to port.

The U.S. Seventh Fleet called their allies in the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force. Within minutes, Japan scrambled four aircraft: a P-3C Orion, an HSS-2B helicopter, and two giant four-engine Shin Meiwa US-1A amphibious flying boats.

Standard military transports need a concrete runway. Japan's US-1A flying boat was engineered to land directly on open ocean waves up to ten feet high.

While the American nuclear cruiser held position in the swells, the orange-and-white Japanese seaplane dropped out of the sky, landed directly on the open Pacific, and taxied right up beside the USS California.

Crews transferred Petty Officer Henderson across the waves by boat into the Japanese seaplane. The Japanese pilots gunned all four turboprop engines, lifted off the water, and rushed him to Atsugi and U.S. Naval Hospital Yokosuka in time for surgery.

It was the first open-ocean seaplane transfer in U.S.-Japan history, all for one young American sailor.

yokosuka.t: My uncle fixed American warships for 41 years. He was a welder at the US Navy base in Yokosuka. He started at 19. He barely spoke English. He didn't need to. H…
yokosuka.tx:
My uncle fixed American warships for 41 years.

He was a welder at the US Navy base in Yokosuka. He started at 19. He barely spoke English. He didn't need to. He spoke steel.

Destroyers. Cruisers. An aircraft carrier, more times than he can count. If a ship in the Seventh Fleet had a seam, there's a decent chance my uncle welded it.

He never met most of the sailors who sailed on them. He just knew they came home safe. Because the seams held.

Last spring, he retired.

He expected a cake in the break room. Maybe a certificate.

Instead, when he walked out of the shop on his last day, there were sailors lined up on both sides of the pier. In dress uniform.

A boatswain raised a whistle to his lips.

My uncle had no idea what was happening. Someone had to explain it to him later.

In the US Navy, when a sailor retires after a long career, they "pipe him ashore." Sideboys line up. The whistle sounds. Everyone salutes.

It's an honor the Navy gives its own.

They gave it to a Japanese welder.

My uncle walked between them slowly. Every few steps, he stopped and bowed. They held their salute the entire time.

At the end of the line, the captain shook his hand and said something my uncle didn't understand.

That night, he asked me to translate it.

"Fair winds and following seas."

He made me write it down in Japanese letters, so he could say it right.

Now, every time we leave his house, he walks us to the door and says the only English sentence he knows by heart.

"Fair winds and following seas."

yokosuka.t: On September 21, 2001, while smoke was still rising from the rubble of the World Trade Center in New York, the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk prepared to sail…
yokosuka.tx:
On September 21, 2001, while smoke was still rising from the rubble of the World Trade Center in New York, the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk prepared to sail out of Yokosuka, Japan, into war.

Every sailor on board knew the danger they faced before even reaching the open ocean.

Why was leaving Tokyo Bay the most dangerous moment of the voyage? Because to reach the Pacific, the giant carrier had to squeeze through the narrow Uraga Channel, a crowded waterway packed with hundreds of small civilian boats where a single suicide vessel loaded with explosives could strike at point-blank range.

As the Kitty Hawk slipped her moorings that morning, the American crew looked out from the flight deck in stunned silence.

Gray destroyers of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force and white patrol boats of the Japan Coast Guard had formed a tight steel wall directly along both sides of the American carrier.

The Japanese captains positioned their own hulls between the USS Kitty Hawk and all oncoming boat traffic. If a terrorist boat tried to ram the American carrier, it would have to hit a Japanese ship first.

Then the American sailors looked at the rocky cliffs of Yokosuka and Kannonzaki Lighthouse.

Thousands of Japanese citizens, base workers, and families were standing shoulder to shoulder along the shore, waving American flags and holding up hand-painted banners that read "We Are With You."

In her hour of deepest grief, America did not sail out of Japan alone. Japan sailed as her shield.

yokosuka.t: September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack. Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens be…
yokosuka.tx:
September 12, 2001. Armed US sailors lock down the main gate of Yokosuka Naval Base and brace for another attack.

Within hours, a crowd of Japanese citizens begins walking toward the concrete barriers.

The commander of the base was a 48 year old US Navy Captain. His name was Robert Francois.

Hours earlier, on the night of September 11 in Japan, four hijacked planes had struck New York, the Pentagon, and Pennsylvania. Half a world away, the 20,000 Americans stationed at Yokosuka, home of the US Seventh Fleet, were cut off from home. Phone lines to the United States were jammed. Young sailors stood watch in full combat gear behind steel barricades, terrified for their families and expecting further strikes.

They felt completely alone.

Then the sun came up over Tokyo Bay.

One by one, residents from the city of Yokosuka walked up to the armed guards at the main gate. An elderly woman bowed in silence and placed a bouquet of white chrysanthemums on the pavement.

Not a word.

Then came schoolchildren carrying strings of 1,000 folded paper cranes.

By afternoon, the security barrier was buried under a wall of fresh flowers, candles, American flags, and handwritten notes. On scraps of paper, Japanese neighbors had written in careful English: "We cry with you" and "America, stay strong."

Here's where it gets even more moving. Ten days later, on September 21, when the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk departed Yokosuka, thousands of Japanese citizens and Maritime Self Defense Force sailors lined the harbor waving American flags to see the crew off.

Captain Robert Francois retired from the Navy in 2003 after 30 years of service. Ten years after 9/11, when the March 2011 tsunami devastated northern Japan, the Seventh Fleet sailed straight from Yokosuka to launch Operation Tomodachi, rescuing thousands of Japanese families.

On the darkest morning in modern American history, a city that once fought the US Navy made sure its sailors never cried alone.

yokosuka.t: October, 1989. Battleship New Jersey is part of the American battle line during a fleet exercise, followed by USS Missouri and the nuclear-powered guided missi…
yokosuka.tx:
October, 1989. Battleship New Jersey is part of the American battle line during a fleet exercise, followed by USS Missouri and the nuclear-powered guided missile cruiser USS Long Beach, with screening ships astern. The photo was taken from the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier USS Enterprise off the coast of Yokosuka, Japan.

Ships in a formation like this one worked together, each adding its own strengths and helping to protect the others. Even a battleship with nine 16-inch guns relied on the ships around it.

Nearby ships and aircraft were tracked on board in the Combat Engagement Center. Big ships can’t turn on a dime, so knowing what was nearby mattered for coordination and safety. The CEC is one of the most restored areas on the ship and a must-see when you visit.

yokosuka.t: I have an urgent Halloween question for Americans. Tonight, my wife and I walked past an American neighbor's house in Yokosuka. No one was home, but there was…
yokosuka.tx:
I have an urgent Halloween question for Americans.

Tonight, my wife and I walked past an American neighbor's house in Yokosuka.

No one was home, but there was a giant plastic bowl full of candy sitting on a chair outside the front door.

Taped to the bowl was a handwritten sign that said: "Happy Halloween! Please take one."

My wife stopped walking. She stared at the unattended bowl in pure disbelief.

In Japan, we have unmanned vegetable stands in the countryside where people leave coins in a box. We understand the honor system for adults buying radishes.

"Wait," my wife whispered. "They left five pounds of chocolate in front of unsupervised children in the dark?"

She looked around the street as if looking for hidden cameras.

"Is this a trap?" she asked me. "Is the homeowner hiding in the bushes to test the moral character of the neighborhood kids?"

Please tell me the truth. Does the second kid who walks up to that bowl actually take just one piece? Or does that bowl become completely empty in four minutes?

yokosuka.t: The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG) tied up in Yokosuka, Japan, on Monday, a week after the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group departed from the…
yokosuka.tx:
The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG) tied up in Yokosuka, Japan, on Monday, a week after the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group departed from the same base to participate in exercise Keen Sword 27. Both are reportedly destined for the Middle East, two U.S. officials confirmed to Fox News, which would place three CSGs and two ARGs in U.S. Central Command sometime in November, unless a group leaves before their arrival. More than 10 guided-missile destroyers are also operating independently in the region, as the U.S. beefs up force posture ahead of the possibility of renewed hostilities against Iran.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the world, the USS Ronald Reagan remotely controlled an MQ-25A Stingray tanker drone thousands of miles away for the first time, and the Navy announced that USS Abraham Lincoln, which just returned from a historic deployment, will conduct a homeport shift to Bremerton, Washington.

yokosuka.t: In Ginza, ordering sushi that is not on the menu gets you a polite refusal. In my neighborhood in Yokosuka, a giant young marine from Texas walked into our tin…
yokosuka.tx:
In Ginza, ordering sushi that is not on the menu gets you a polite refusal.

In my neighborhood in Yokosuka, a giant young marine from Texas walked into our tiny eight seat sushi bar, nervous and sweating.

He wanted to order a Tekka Maki, the classic tuna roll.

Instead, he pointed at the glass case and asked the 68 year old master for a "Texas Roll."

Master Watanabe did not blink. He did not correct him.

He sliced a piece of bluefin tuna twice as thick as usual, added pickled jalapeno from his own lunch, and shaped it with two sharp claps of his hands.

"One Texas Roll," the master said, placing it on the cedar board.

That marine came back every Friday for two years until his deployment ended.

When a new batch of sailors walked in last night and asked what the house special was, Master Watanabe pointed to a wooden plaque on the wall.

It is the most expensive item on the menu now.

kadena.t: On July 22, 2012, a United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon pilot out of Misawa Air Base had to eject into the freezing North Pacific Ocean 250 miles nort…
kadena.tx:
On July 22, 2012, a United States Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon pilot out of Misawa Air Base had to eject into the freezing North Pacific Ocean 250 miles northeast of Hokkaido, Japan.

For the next six hours, the American pilot, callsign JEST 73, floated alone in a tiny one-man life raft, using his own flight helmet by hand to bail icy water out so he would not sink.

Above the clouds, three U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotankers from Kadena and McConnell refused to leave him, circling in shifts while relaying his coordinates to Japanese and American rescue controllers.

One hundred miles away, Captain Mike Gruninger and Second Mate Jim Dowling aboard the American container ship MV Manukai ordered maximum engine RPMs and turned their giant ship around.

At the exact same moment, a Japanese fishing boat named the Hokko Maru raced through the swells toward the same spot.

Because the 700-foot American container ship was too tall to pluck a man safely from a rubber raft in rolling waves, the Japanese fishermen on the Hokko Maru pulled the shivering American pilot from the sea and brought him right alongside the Manukai's lowered gangway ladder.

All twenty-one American sailors lined the rails cheering as he climbed aboard, where the ship's satellite phone was already dialed to his wife and two little girls.

Tucker Carlson reports that Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Donald Trump to launch a nuclear strike on Iran. Before that idea gains any ground in Washington, its consequences need to be understood. More than 180 countries renounced nuclear weapons under a set of explicit promises. A nuclear attack on Iran would show those promises to be worthless.

The bargain is written into the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty itself. Under Article II, non-nuclear-weapon states agreed not to acquire nuclear arms. In return, they were promised three things: the inalienable right to peaceful nuclear energy, good-faith negotiations toward disarmament by the nuclear powers, and - when the treaty was extended indefinitely - assurances that nuclear weapons would not be used against them, noted by the Security Council in Resolution 984. In Iran’s case, the first promise has already been broken: its peaceful programme has been sanctioned and bombed. The second has gone unmet for decades. A nuclear strike would break the third.

The regime urging this strike has never accepted any part of that bargain. Israel refuses to join the NPT, has never acknowledged the arsenal it built at Dimona, and has ignored Security Council Resolution 487 calling on it to place its nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards. When Mordechai Vanunu exposed the programme, Israeli agents abducted him in Rome and he spent 18 years in prison. Under the Begin Doctrine, Israel claims the right to bomb any state in the region it suspects of seeking the capability it already possesses, while demanding total transparency from its neighbours and accepting none for itself. At the same time, Israel stands accused of genocide and of widespread war crimes and crimes against humanity. Its forces have repeatedly violated the sovereignty of neighbouring states through cross-border strikes and occupations, and it has pursued an openly aggressive posture across the region. Its prime minister is wanted by the International Criminal Court. This is the war criminal now urging Washington to use the most destructive weapon ever built against a member of the treaty his regime has spent half a century evading.

Iran’s record points the other way. It negotiated the JCPOA, which the Security Council endorsed unanimously in Resolution 2231, and the IAEA confirmed its compliance in report after report. Washington walked away anyway. When Iran returned to the table, it was attacked twice: days before a scheduled round with U.S. envoys, and hours after talks in Geneva that Oman’s foreign minister said had brought the two sides close to a genuine agreement.

Article X allows any party to withdraw if extraordinary events related to the treaty have jeopardised its supreme interests. A nuclear attack on a member that negotiated, complied, and kept returning to diplomacy would hand that argument to every other member. Islamic countries will rightly see an ethno-supremacist and racist ideology behind this use of nuclear weapons. A nuclear strike against a Muslim-majority nation, urged by a regime that has long defined itself in ethno-religious terms and that has never accepted the restraints of the NPT, would be read not as a narrow security measure but as the expression of a deeper hierarchy of peoples. That perception would further erode confidence in the treaty among its Islamic members and accelerate momentum toward withdrawal. The treaty rests on a single premise: that a state can give up the bomb and still be safe. If that premise fails in Iran, parliaments, politicians, and publics across the membership will start asking whether staying in serves their security. Some governments will decide that it does not. Withdrawals, individual or collective, would follow, and the non-proliferation regime would simply not survive them.

dimona.t: ⛔️ Did Mossad kill Kennedy? Where the allegation comes from, and what the evidence shows‼️ ▪️ The theory mainly comes from Michael Collins Piper's 1994 book "F…
dimona.tx:
⛔️ Did Mossad kill Kennedy? Where the allegation comes from, and what the evidence shows‼️

▪️ The theory mainly comes from Michael Collins Piper's 1994 book "Final Judgment," which claims Mossad worked alongside the CIA and organized crime to assassinate Kennedy
▪️ Piper's main motive argument is JFK's clash with Israel over its secret nuclear program at Dimona
▪️ That clash is real and documented. In a May 18, 1963 letter to Ben-Gurion, Kennedy demanded regular US inspections of Dimona and warned of "the disturbing effects on world stability" of an Israeli nuclear weapon
▪️ Piper says his research began with a single secondhand informant quote from 1963 about "new backers" of anti-Castro exiles, and he admits there's no forensic proof
▪️ The 2025 JFK file releases include FBI memos on CIA counterintelligence chief James Angleton's close contacts with Israeli intelligence, but they show liaison work, not a role in the killing
▪️ No official inquiry has found any Israeli link: not the Warren Commission (1964), not the House Select Committee (1979), and not the Review Board
▪️ The Warren Commission found that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone. The 1979 House committee concluded there was "probably" a conspiracy but pointed to no foreign government
▪️ Mainstream JFK researchers, including those who believe in a conspiracy, leave Piper's work out, and outlets like The Jerusalem Post describe it as an antisemitic trope‼️

🔺Sources:
•Kennedy's May 1963 letter to Ben-Gurion on Dimona (US State Department historian)
•JFK Library: Israel's nuclear program files, 1963
•National Archives 2025 release: FBI memo on Angleton and Israeli intelligence
•Michael Collins Piper (background on the author)

fordow.tx:
🇮🇷|Araghchi to Merz: "There Will Be No More Red Lines." Germany's Welcome of the Airstrikes Has Been Noted. And So Has Its Bill.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Saturday, 31 October 2026: "When U.S. and Zionist airstrikes against Iran began last year, Mr. Merz welcomed these attacks, describing them as the execution of 'Europe's dirty work.'"

Then the line that matters: "A sum of 100 billion euros cannot be compared to the decisive and devastating response that the Iranian armed forces will deliver to anyone who dares to violate our nation's sovereignty; there will be no more 'red lines.'"

The Foreign Minister named the co-belligerent.

Friedrich Merz is not an observer. He is the German Chancellor. When US and Israeli aircraft bombed Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan in June 2025, Merz did not call for restraint. He welcomed the strikes. He called them Europe's dirty work, a phrasing that admits the continent wanted the bombing done and preferred that someone else's pilots do it. Araghchi has now put that admission on the record from the Iranian foreign ministry's own account.

That is not a diplomatic exchange. That is a charge sheet.

Read what "no more red lines" means.

For two decades Iran operated inside a restraint doctrine. It stayed in the NPT. It accepted IAEA inspections. It negotiated the JCPOA. It absorbed the US withdrawal from that deal in 2018. It absorbed the assassination of its scientists. It absorbed the bombing of its safeguarded facilities and the IAEA's silence about who dropped the bombs. Every stage of that restraint was a red line Iran chose not to cross.

Araghchi has just announced the end of that doctrine. "No more red lines" is not a threat aimed at one country. It is the formal abandonment of the restraint architecture. It tells Berlin, Washington, and Tel Aviv that the calculation that kept Iran inside limits no longer applies.

The 100 billion euros is the German rearmament bill, and Araghchi sized it against the wrong column.

The 100 billion euro figure is the German defence fund Berlin created to rebuild the Bundeswehr. Araghchi compared it to the response the Iranian armed forces will deliver. His point is arithmetic, not rhetoric: money buys hardware, and hardware does not answer what Iran answers with. German defence procurement is a budget line. Iranian retaliation is a doctrine that has already been demonstrated against Saudi airports at Najran, Khamis Mushait, and Abha.

The deeper layer Berlin does not want examined.

Germany presents itself as a diplomatic actor in the Iran file. It was an E3 member of the JCPOA negotiations. It signed the deal. Then it stood with Washington after Washington destroyed the deal. Then it welcomed the bombing campaign that hit the facilities the deal had verified.

Berlin supplied the political cover. The United States and Israel supplied the aircraft. Merz called it Europe's dirty work because he understood the division of labour. Germany wanted the Iranian nuclear programme bombed without German aircraft in the sky and without German crews in the cockpits. It got what it wanted and then told its public it was a spectator.

Araghchi has refused the spectator framing. He has put Merz in the co-belligerent column, by name, from the foreign ministry's official account.

The contradiction Washington and Berlin cannot resolve.

Germany is not an NPT nuclear weapons state. It shelters under NATO's nuclear umbrella. It hosts US nuclear weapons at Büchel. It lectures Iran about NPT compliance while sitting inside a nuclear sharing arrangement. It welcomed the bombing of safeguarded facilities inside a non-nuclear-weapons state that was, at the moment of the bombing, under IAEA inspection.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors from Iran in June 2025 because of the safety risk of the strikes. The Security Council has since drafted resolutions blaming Iran for the resulting loss of continuity. Germany voted for the architecture that produced that outcome

Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated set

fordow.tx:
This is hysterical nonsense. 
Trump and Netanyahu will not nuke Pickaxe Mountain. 

Trump has indicated on numerous occasions he despises nuclear weapons and would prefer “denuclearization.” Israel does not want to be the country that breaks the norm against nuclear weapons use and triggers a race for nukes in its region. 

What may be on the table is disabling Tehran’s access to Pickaxe’s tunnel entrances—which the United States did rather effectively using 30 Tomahawk missiles against the Esfahan nuclear complex—in 2025. The Esfahan tunnels house highly enriched uranium and a new enrichment plant. The regime has not restored access all this time, and blocking access has allowed for monitoring to detect such activity.

Pickaxe has the potential to serve as a new enrichment and weaponization facility, more deeply buried that Fordow. Iran reportedly moved surviving centrifuges there in the fall of 2025. It hasn’t been constructing the facility in recent weeks, having fortified the tunnels against a possible strike. 

Let’s remember: Tehran could resolve all of this tomorrow by simply letting the IAEA go there or agreeing to verifiably dismantle it—something Iran has refused for years. It has also been continuing work on other undeclared sites struck during 2025 and 2026. 

It would not be surprising if the U.S. and Israel act against Pickaxe to prevent the Iranians from restoring a nuclear weapons pathway—indeed, it would be irresponsible to leave such a decision to their successors. 

But it won’t be a nuclear strike.

natanz.tx:
Earlier this summer, the wonderful editors at @thebafflermag asked me if I wanted to contribute an essay for a forthcoming issue.

I said I wanted to write about Iranian bricks.

Iran's remarkable brick architecture has become something of a meme. Everyday there's a new picture circulating online of a beautiful brick edifice in some Iranian city (often courtesy of @SustainableTall).

But why is Iran, a country dealing with so many traumas, the site of the most innovative and ambitious brick architecture in the world?

That's the question I set out to answer in this essay, which starts with a visit to the mudbrick village of Abyaneh, just over the ridge from the nuclear site at Natanz.

pickaxe.tx:
Tucker, you’re telling millions of people we’re days away from nuclear war, but your story falls apart when you check the record.

You claim a nuclear strike is the only military option at Pickaxe Mountain. Wrong. Conventional strikes can collapse entrances, destroy utilities, and disable access. CSIS has discussed exactly that. October satellite analysis also found no evidence the site was actively enriching uranium.

And blowing up a mountain doesn’t magically erase enriched uranium or decades of nuclear expertise. Material can survive buried under rubble and potentially be recovered. You can destroy machinery without destroying the underlying capability.

If you have evidence of an imminent nuclear strike, publish it.

parchin.t: An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on nat…
parchin.tx:
An Islamic Republic official admits the regime lied about the massive damage inflicted by U.S. and Israeli strikes, blaming explosions at military sites on natural events such as thunder and lightning.

Mohammad Sadegh Koushki, a hardline regime figure appearing on state television, described the deception openly. Israeli strikes on the Kermanshah drone base were publicly blamed on thunder and lightning, while repeated attacks on missile facilities and other sensitive military sites were never announced.

This was not an isolated cover story. It was part of a systematic campaign to hide the scale of the regime’s military losses while exaggerating its remaining strength and supposed victories.

“Gas leaks” are another standard cover story used when explosions occur at or near sensitive military, missile and IRGC-linked facilities. Like the lightning excuse, the explanation allows the regime to disguise a possible attack or act of sabotage as an ordinary domestic accident.

In June 2020, a massive nighttime explosion near the Parchin military complex was officially blamed on a gas leak at a storage facility in a public area. Satellite imagery later revealed extensive damage and scorch marks at the adjacent Khojir missile-production complex, directing attention toward a facility associated with missile propellants rather than the harmless location described by the regime.

The same pattern resurfaced after the July 2025 explosion at the Pamchal 9 complex, a residential building connected to the Armed Forces Judicial Organization. State and judiciary media blamed owner negligence and a gas leak. Residents reportedly disputed the explanation, saying the building was not connected to the municipal gas network and that the damage across several floors did not resemble an ordinary domestic explosion.

Other explosions near military and industrial facilities have been attributed to gas leaks, aging infrastructure or routine accidents. In some cases, regime-linked outlets initially raised the possibility of Israeli involvement before deleting those references and adopting the official accident narrative.

When U.S. and Israeli strikes damaged drone bases, missile-production facilities, air defences, naval assets and command centres, the regime responded with silence, weather excuses and restrictions on reporting from the affected areas. Evidence of destruction was concealed from Iranians because acknowledging it would expose the failure of the military system that consumed enormous national resources while proving unable to protect itself.

The regime simultaneously manufactured stories of overwhelming retaliation. State television and IRGC-linked outlets claimed Iranian missiles had destroyed strategic Israeli sites, devastated American forces and achieved extraordinary success rates. Many of these claims relied on recycled footage, manipulated imagery, fabricated casualty figures or targets that independent evidence showed remained operational.

The strategy was simple. Hide Iranian losses, invent enemy losses and preserve the illusion that the regime remained in control.

The actual damage was substantial, although American assessments differed over its permanence. U.S. Central Command described severe degradation across Iran’s missile, drone, naval and defence-industrial infrastructure. It reported that launch rates had fallen dramatically and that large portions of production capacity and major naval assets had been destroyed.

More cautious American intelligence assessments concluded that Iran retained significant missile stocks, mobile launchers and access to many underground facilities. That means the regime was badly damaged but not disarmed. It still possesses dangerous capabilities and could rebuild parts of its arsenal over time.

Both assessments, however, contradict the Islamic Republic’s claim that its forces emerged largely intact or even stronger.

Koushki’s admission reveals why official Iranian accounts cannot be trus

Last time $KRKNF traded below $3 USD was mid-September 2025. Market cap then was ~US$0.9B, and it's ~US$1.1B now. But the company is not the same size.

Sept 2025: A battery and sonar company. C$26M quarters, C$91M in cash, and a 2025 guide of C$120-135M revenue.

Oct 2026: Kraken plus Covelya's six subsidiaries (Sonardyne, Voyis, EIVA, Wavefront, Forcys, Chelsea), bought for C$615M at ~2.3x sales. The 2026 guide is C$290-320M revenue and C$65-75M EBITDA, with only half a year of Covelya in it. Power, sonar, navigation, positioning and imaging for the same hull, from one supplier.

Demand: C$355M in announced 2026 orders. Almost 10 new UUV battery OEM customers in ~18 months across North America, Europe and Asia. A long-term battery supply deal with an XL-UUV builder, with batteries already shipping to two other XL-UUV makers. Canada committed C$816M to the Coast Guard, including subsea drones, and announced a C$1.2B oceans package with seabed mapping.

Hormuz: Iran mined the strait. With the last Bahrain-based Avenger minesweepers and MH-53E sweep helicopters already retired, underwater drones did the hunting. 100+ suspected mines found by August.

Corsair: In June, a Saronic Corsair drone boat pulled two downed Apache pilots out of the water off Oman. In July, three Corsairs struck Bandar Abbas naval base, the first US combat use of attack drone boats. The Navy holds a US$392M Corsair contract.

REMUS: HII has delivered 750+ REMUS drones to 30+ countries. The Navy exercised another Lionfish (REMUS 300) production option in July on a contract for up to 200 vehicles. HII expanded its Pocasset plant 25% in September.

Anduril: The Rhode Island Dive-LD line is built for ~200 hulls a year, with full capacity targeted for end of 2027. A second line for Dive-XL is planned for year-end. Iran captured a Dive-LD in September, and Anduril's founder called it a mass-produced attritable sub. Attritable hulls get replaced.

Sept 13: A Mk48 torpedo launched from an uncrewed sub for the first time. The next phase, Project CUTLASS, runs on Anduril's Dive-XL, which is likely proceeding under DIU's CAMP program. Every armed hull still needs navigation, power and sonar.

⛔️ The toll of the Saudi-led air war on Yemen's civilians‼️

▪️ About 9,000 civilians were killed in the Saudi-led coalition's air campaign from 2015 to 2022, according to the ACLED conflict monitor
▪️ The Yemen Data Project recorded more than 25,000 air raids before the April 2022 truce
▪️ The UN found that coalition airstrikes caused about 61% of all civilian casualties, more than any other cause
▪️ UNDP estimates about 377,000 people died because of the war by the end of 2021, most of them from hunger and disease
▪️ Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport in July 2026, its first strike on the Houthis since the truce, according to HRW

bab-al-mandab.tx:
US-Iran: The Prospects for Peace Are Dim

The US and Iran have been engaged in on-again, off-again skirmishes in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz ever since large-scale fighting came to a halt back in April. A ceasefire understanding reached in June failed to produce a lasting settlement, and the prospect of renewed major combat operations continues to loom over the Middle East. The consequences for energy security remain significant, with restrictions and attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continuing to disrupt oil markets, while renewed conflict between Yemen’s Ansarullah movement, or Houthis, and Saudi Arabia has heightened risks to Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

bab-al-mandab.tx:
💢🇾🇪 UPDATE: Ansarallah forces have taken the al-Maqatirah district administration building and the district's hilltop fortress in Yemen's southern Lahj province, bringing them within 5 kilometers (~3 miles) of the center of neighboring Tur al-Baha, according to a Yemeni commentator aligned with the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council. 

Saudi outlets claim the Giants Brigades, a UAE-built force, and Saudi Arabia's Homeland Shield forces, both fighting for the council, have instead retaken positions and contained the advance. Drop Site could not independently confirm either account.

The push threatens to encircle the council's forces in the coastal pocket they hold at the Bab al-Mandab Strait. With Ansarallah already controlling the high ground to the north and the Red Sea coast to the west, taking Tur al-Baha and pushing south on the main road from Taiz to Aden would sever the routes that link the pocket to Aden, the council's base and the main source of its reinforcements and supplies. 

Sharing the report, Ansarallah-aligned commentator Hussain al-Bukhaiti suggested Ansarallah could soon capture Ras al-Ara port on the Gulf of Aden, comparing it to Ansarallah's rapid seizure of the Red Sea port of Mocha on Sept. 10. Taking Ras al-Ara would put Ansarallah on both sides of the strait.

▪️@bonzerbarry contributed to this report.

bab-al-mandab.t: 🚨🇺🇸🇸🇦 In a recent New York Times opinion piece, Saudi Ambassador Reema Bandar Al-Saud @rbalsaud made a striking comparison between the fight against ISIS and t…

qt.t:
The terrorist Houthi militias have shown the world what they are capable of. Their threat extends far beyond Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

In @nytopinion, I explain why the international community can no longer afford to underestimate them.

nytimes.com/2026/10/27/opi…

bab-al-mandab.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇸🇦 In a recent New York Times opinion piece, Saudi Ambassador Reema Bandar Al-Saud @rbalsaud made a striking comparison between the fight against ISIS and the challenge posed by the terrorist Houthis:

“ISIS was defeated by local forces backed by a coalition of more than 80 nations. The Houthis can be defeated the same way. It is Yemen’s fight to lead.”

Back in 2014–2015, when ISIS was tearing through Iraq and Syria, the world didn’t just throw together a military coalition. What happened was a rare alignment of self-interest. Countries that normally disagreed on almost everything recognized that the cost of doing nothing was higher than the cost of cooperating.

The Houthis, a terrorist group, have demonstrated capabilities that pose regional and international security concerns, with Iranian support playing a significant role. They’ve launched more than a thousand ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia. They’ve threatened the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical chokepoint for global trade. Their activities have also raised concerns about weapons proliferation, regional militancy, and the recruitment and indoctrination of children.

A disruption to Saudi energy production or export routes could raise fuel, transport, and manufacturing costs worldwide, feeding inflation and squeezing households and businesses far beyond the region.

With ISIS, the death toll and refugee waves hit European and American communities hard enough to force the issue. Much of the human cost of the Houthi threat, by contrast, has fallen on Yemenis and Saudis, while many foreign capitals continue to treat it as a regional problem.

She’s not just saying we need another coalition of more than 80 nations. She’s pointing to a lesson from the fight against ISIS: international cooperation becomes possible when enough countries recognize that the threat extends beyond any single region.

By the time a major disruption to shipping drives up prices for consumers in Chicago or Hamburg, or advances in missile technology create a more immediate threat to distant countries, the cost of responding could be much higher.

Saudi Arabia is working with Yemeni partners, helping counter weapons smuggling, restricting financial channels, and providing humanitarian assistance. Countries should designate the Houthis as a terrorist organization, cut off their funding, intercept weapons shipments at sea, and strengthen support for Yemen’s legitimate government.

Saudi Arabia has a legitimate interest in defending its people and territory and preventing Yemen from becoming a permanent platform for cross-border attacks and regional instability. At the same time, lasting security cannot be built on military pressure alone. It requires a viable Yemeni state, functioning institutions, humanitarian relief, and a political future in which Yemenis, not armed factions backed by outside powers, determine their country’s direction.

Any effective response must be coordinated, grounded in international law, attentive to civilian protection, and paired with a credible path toward peace.

Saudi Arabia should not have to wait for the rest of the world to feel the danger before that danger is acknowledged.

Saudi Arabia’s security, regional security, Yemen’s stability, global energy security, and the freedom of international navigation are inseparable parts of that challenge.

PEACE IS NEVER SECURED BY IGNORING THE THREAT.

suez.t: Oct 31, 1956. An Egyptian warship sails in alone to bombard an Israeli city. By breakfast, she has a new flag and a new name. Ibrahim el Awal had a long histor…
suez.tx:
Oct 31, 1956. An Egyptian warship sails in alone to bombard an Israeli city. By breakfast, she has a new flag and a new name.

Ibrahim el Awal had a long history before that night. She was built as HMS Mendip, a British destroyer that fought in World War II. Later she was loaned to Nationalist China, then sold to Egypt.

On Oct 29, 1956, Israel invaded the Sinai, the start of the Suez Crisis. The next night, Egypt sent Ibrahim el Awal alone toward Haifa, Israel's main port, to shell its oil installations.

At about 3:30 a.m. on Oct 31, she opened fire. Over the next 20 minutes or so she fired around 200 shells at the city. They did little damage and killed no one.

Anchored in Haifa harbor was a French destroyer, Kersaint, part of the secret British and French plan to retake the Suez Canal. She fired back. No hits, but the Egyptian ship turned and ran northwest.

Two Israeli destroyers, Eilat and Yafo, went after her. The chase went on for hours. The Israeli ships fired hundreds of rounds, but their gunners were inexperienced and scored few hits.

At dawn, two Israeli Air Force Ouragan jets arrived and hit her with rockets, knocking out her generator and rudder. Dead in the water, Ibrahim el Awal surrendered just after 7 a.m. Two of her crew had been killed and eight wounded.

Her crew tried to scuttle her. The valves were rusted shut.

Eilat towed her into Haifa, the city she had just shelled. About 200 Egyptian sailors were taken prisoner.

The Israeli Navy repaired her and commissioned her as INS Haifa.

There's a grim twist. The destroyer Eilat, which towed her in, was sunk by Egyptian missiles in 1967, the first ship ever sunk by ship-launched missiles.

Eritrea’s Coveted Geopolitical Location and Irreplaceable Strategic Role in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa

Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the State of Eritrea

29 October 2026

Eritrea’s location along the Red Sea and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has long made it a vital crossroads linking Africa, the Middle East, and global shipping routes. Since the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, its coastline has underpinned a major artery of international trade and energy flows. Today, as conflicts in Yemen, Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia threaten regional stability, Eritrea’s relative cohesion and independent foreign policy give it outsized importance for maritime security and regional order.

Eritrea’s strategic weight goes beyond geography. It stems from a consistent emphasis on sovereignty, resistance to external pressure, and support for littoral-state cooperation to secure the Red Sea. In a Horn of Africa marked by state fragility and competing external interests, Asmara’s posture—acknowledged by partners including Egypt, Sudan, and Somalia—positions it as a stabilizing actor whose choices affect security and commerce well beyond its borders.
