Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, member of Ansarallah's Supreme Political Council, criticized Saudi Arabia's claims of seeking regional de-escalation through its defense minister's visit to Tehran, arguing that Riyadh's diplomatic rhetoric contradicts its continued war, blockade, and occupation of Yemen.
——
In a statement responding to the Saudi Foreign Ministry, al-Houthi outlined the following positions:

• Riyadh cannot claim to promote regional peace and security while continuing its military attacks, blockade, and occupation of Yemen. Houthi said Saudi Arabia's actions directly contradict its stated commitment to de-escalation.

• Saudi Arabia must halt its aggression, lift the blockade, withdraw from occupied Yemeni territory, and compensate Yemen for destruction caused since 2015. He stressed that if Saudi attacks cease, Yemeni operations will also stop and normal life can resume.

• Houthi criticized the so-called 'Mecca Defense Pact', arguing that it seeks to address what its members call the Iranian crisis while concealing what he described as outright aggression against Iran. He warned that Saudi Arabia's previous alliances had failed and that Riyadh had even turned against former partners.

• He condemned Egypt and its parliament for supporting the defense of Saudi Arabia, arguing that such a position effectively amounts to declaring war on Yemen. He warned that Egypt risks repeating its military entanglement in Yemen during the 1960s, exhausting its forces and potentially leaving Sinai vulnerable to Israeli expansion and plans to displace Palestinians into Egyptian territory.

• Houthi stressed that Yemen does not fear new military alliances but warned these countries against supporting Saudi attacks, the blockade, or the occupation of Yemen. He urged them instead to direct their cooperation against Israel, which he said is waging war across Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran while also threatening Egypt.

• He rejected claims that Yemen poses a threat to regional waterways, maintaining that Yemen's position contributes to protecting Bab al-Mandab, the Suez Canal, and the wider Arab and Islamic region.

• He reaffirmed that Yemen's political and military position has remained unchanged since 2015, arguing that US, British, and Israeli intelligence agencies manufacture fears of unspecified threats to perpetuate divisions and conflict within the Arab and Islamic world.

suez.nm: The Daily Great War at Sea
suez.tx:
Requin

Terrible-class ironclad barbette ship (1885)

Originally mounted two 16.5 in. guns, the largest ever mounted on a French capital ship. Refitted in the late 1890's with better armor and armaments, she was employed as guard ship at Cherbourg and a gunnery training ship at Toulon. Placed in reserve at Bizerte in 1913, Requin was actually being refitted again to be utilized as a coastal defense ship when war broke out. 
Transferred to Ismailia to guard the Suez Canal, Requin engaged Ottoman forces in 1915 along the canal, driving them back with fire from her main gun. 
Moved to the Palestine coast in October 1917 to be used offensively against Ottoman positions there. Damaged by Ottoman artillery in November 1917 she returned to Port Said for repairs and spent the rest of the war guarding the canal. Scrapped in 1921.

Understand what a compliant China would have meant.

Not just strategically. Economically.

The largest consumer market on earth, opened on American terms.

The manufacturing base of Asia, structured to serve American capital.

A military ally anchoring the Western Pacific.

A permanent American presence at the edge of the Soviet Union's eastern flank.

This was not a fantasy. This was the plan.

This was what Washington spent billions supporting the Kuomintang to achieve.

The plan failed. Completely, irreversibly, and publicly.

And the alternative that emerged, a China explicitly committed to its own development on its own terms, hostile to the architecture of American-managed Asian order, has never stopped being, at the core of American strategic anxiety, the thing that went wrong.

Everything since, the refusal to recognize the PRC for three decades, the Korean War, the Taiwan Strait crises, the American war in Vietnam, the encirclement strategy, the current technology war, is the long aftermath of 1949.

The plan failed.

Washington never fully accepted that the failure was permanent.

taiwan-strait.t: What if the most revealing evidence about Nixon's position on Taiwan was never published in the 1972 Shanghai Communique? A TOP SECRET White House briefing pre…

qt.t:
48 hours before Nixon landed in China, Kissinger sent him a TOP SECRET memo.

Dated February 19, 1972, it offered a remarkably candid psychological and strategic assessment of Chairman Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai.

A few lines caught my eye:

"They see history on their side."

In the previous pages, Kissinger recognized something remarkable about China's leaders: they were deeply ideological, yet extraordinarily pragmatic. They understood the long game of history.

But Kissinger also understood something crucial: both men were in their seventies. Time was running out, and they wanted to secure their country's future before leaving the political stage.

He warned Nixon that China would judge America not merely by its words, but by its seriousness, reliability, and willingness to deliver on its commitments.

And then came his chilling final warning:

History might remember Nixon's visit as "a gallant but stillborn venture."

Nixon himself underlined numerous passages in this classified memo.

Two days later, he walked into Mao's study in Beijing's Zhongnanhai.

By the end of the visit, the two countries had issued the Shanghai Communique.

Kissinger had warned of a historic fai

taiwan-strait.tx:
What if the most revealing evidence about Nixon's position on Taiwan was never published in the 1972 Shanghai Communique?

A TOP SECRET White House briefing prepared for his historic China visit contained language far more explicit than the carefully negotiated public statement.

It said Washington would not claim Taiwan's status was undetermined. It would not encourage other countries to make that claim either.

And then there was a handwritten note:
"Taiwan will be settled."

I examined this document at the Nixon Presidential Library about a decade ago.

Now, let's uncover what this remarkable document reveals about one of the most consequential diplomatic agreements of the Cold War.

On February 28, 1972, as President Richard Nixon's historic visit to China drew to a close, Washington and Beijing issued the Shanghai Communique, the first of the three foundational joint communiques that would come to define China-US relations.

Without question, the most important part of the communique was its language on Taiwan.

The US side declared: The United States acknowledges that all Chinese on either side of the Taiwan Strait maintain there is but one China and that Taiwan is a part of China. The United States Government does not challenge that position.

When I was studying US foreign policy at Cornell, I discussed this particular wording with two of my instructors. Both interpreted it as meaning that the United States had been committed to the One China principle and that Taiwan was part of China.

Yet many of Washington's subsequent actions appeared inconsistent with the language of the communique. So they viewed this as a failure by the United States to honor its commitments.

Later, however, while studying at Stanford, I heard a strikingly different interpretation from another professor. She was also a renowned fellow at Hoover and a longtime China specialist who had been reading the People's Daily (人民日报) consistently since the 1970s. And she spent most of her career researching in DC.

She pointed out that Washington's diplomats were often far more deliberate in their choice of words than most people might imagine.

And the key, she explained, lay in just two English words: Acknowledge and Recognize.

In everyday English, acknowledge can mean admitting that something is true, but it can also simply mean being aware of, taking note of, or recognizing the existence of a particular position.

In diplomatic language, however, recognize often carries a stronger implication of formal recognition.

This is why some diplomats in DC confidently claim that the United States has never broken its promises. Their argument is that acknowledge does not go as far as recognize. In their interpretation, Washington merely "heard" that the Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait maintained there was one China and that Taiwan was part of China, without formally endorsing that position as its own.

What did the White House really think about Taiwan behind closed doors? Let's take a closer look at this memo.
-- Neither of us should allow the Taiwan issue to color unduly our developing relationship. There are many areas in which cooperation between our two countries would be to our mutual benefit, and the absence of diplomatic relations due to Taiwan ought not to prevent such cooperation.

In the Legal Status of Taiwan part, A section headed "Your Position" explicitly laid out the stance President Nixon was advised to take on Taiwan.
-- You hope that the assurances which you have already given regarding our policy not to support "two Chinas," "one China, one Taiwan," or the Taiwan independence movement will convince the Chinese of your good intentions.

-- Regarding the status of Taiwan, you have noticed that Chinese on both sides of the Taiwan Strait agree that there is only one China and that Taiwan is a part of it. In this sense we do not maintain that the status of Taiwan is undetermined. There will be no statements from US officials about Ta

qt.t:
Trump is reportedly planning to restart war with Iran after the election.

Some of us have been briefed on the war plan. And while I cannot disclose any details, I can say this: the plan is insane. It will not achieve objectives and will set off a new cycle of escalation.

ras-laffan.tx:
I increasingly believe some level of infrastructure warfare between the US/Israel and Iran, on a scale we haven't yet seen, is inevitable.

Iran, for its part, sees negating this long-threatened card in Trump's playbook as critical to establishing lasting deterrence.

It has signaled that it would retaliate ferociously against regional infrastructure, much of which is far more concentrated and vulnerable than Iran's relatively dispersed critical infrastructure, such its electricity grid.

Many Persian Gulf Arab states and Israel depend on just a handful of desalination plants, power stations, and refineries.

With that said, I wouldn't expect such an infrastructure war to last long, or reach catastrophic levels, largely because I expect Iran would retaliate on a scale that would compel the US to stop quickly (like it did after Iran hit Ras Laffan in March).

Yet if that doesn't happen, the consequences could be disastrous for all sides.

The destruction of critical regional energy infrastructure would greatly exacerbate the existing energy crisis, likely push many economies, including the US, into recession, and deal a devastating blow to the rest of Trump's presidency and his legacy. Whether that prospect has already deterred him, however, remains quite unclear.

ras-laffan.t: 🇷🇺| Putin Holds Up a Mirror: From the Persian Gulf to the Baltic Sea October 2026. Putin poses a question: "Does someone want the Baltic Sea to become like the…
ras-laffan.tx:
🇷🇺| Putin Holds Up a Mirror: From the Persian Gulf to the Baltic Sea

October 2026. Putin poses a question:

"Does someone want the Baltic Sea to become like the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz? I don’t know. We certainly do not."

This isn't mere question, he is pointing to a region already devastated by war, he issues a stark warning to those currently creating the same conditions in the Baltic Sea.

💥 Who Brought the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz "At the Current State"?

Look at the current state of the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz:

U.S. carrier strike groups patrol the Arabian Sea. The U.S. Navy intercepts vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. incites shipowners to enter minefields, while Iran, acting in self-defense layed mines. Seven ships were struck or hit mines within 24 hours. 4.5 million barrels of crude oil go up in flames. Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas facility is struck with precision. Saudi Aramco’s facilities in Yanbu catch fire. The airport in Dammam is shut down. An F-35 in the UAE broadcasts a 7700 emergency squawk code.

This isn't a "natural state of affairs." It is the direct result of the United States waging war on Iran, imposing a naval blockade, goading vessels into prohibited zones, and then accusing Iran of "threatening the freedom of navigation."

The situation in the Persian Gulf and in the Strait of Hormuz is a U.S. creation.

🎯 Who Is Causing the Same situation in the Baltic Sea?

Under the guise of "defense," NATO’s military presence in the Baltic Sea is replicating the U.S. playbook from the Persian Gulf.

NATO exercises in the Baltic are becoming increasingly frequent and larger in scale. NATO warships are venturing ever closer to Russian territorial waters, while NATO reconnaissance aircraft are flying with growing intensity along the borders of Kaliningrad and Belarus. With the accession of Finland and Sweden to NATO, the Baltic Sea has effectively become a "NATO lake," while Russia’s Baltic Fleet finds itself confined to bases in Kaliningrad and St. Petersburg, both surrounded by NATO territory.

This mirrors the situation in the Persian Gulf: one side deploys military forces right at the other’s doorstep, calling it "defense." One side intercepts the other’s merchant vessels, labeling it "sanctions." One side conducts military exercises near the other’s coastline, describing it as "routine training."

Putin asks: Is someone trying to turn the Baltic Sea into another Persian Gulf? He is not saying "Russia wants this"; he is asking if "someone else" does someone located in Washington, in Brussels, or within the NATO chain of command.

📜 Russia’s Response: Not a "Threat," but a "Mirror Image"

Putin says: "We do not want this."

This is not "weakness"; it is "reciprocity." Russia does not want the Baltic Sea to become like the Persian Gulf, a region devastated by war. Kaliningrad serves as one of Russia’s most critical strategic footholds on the Baltic coast, while St. Petersburg acts as the home port for the Baltic Fleet. Furthermore, Russia’s energy exports rely heavily on its Baltic ports.

If the Baltic Sea were to become a Persian Gulf, Russia’s energy exports would be severed, its exclave blockaded, and its fleet trapped in port.

This is a "mirror image," you can't call it escalation.

It is well into Nov 1st in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East...

So WINTER is well on its way and here is the "winter test" you need to be aware of and what Europe’s next six months will look like...

My assessment is that this winter answers much of what happens to the price of diesel, LNG, and energy needs of Europe, and the order in which the costs arrive.

Europe enters November with gas storage at 75% (21 October, ACER), below its nine-year average, after one of the slowest summer refills in 15 years.

Brent rose 13.6% in October, with the front-month contract settling at $117.64 on 30 October.

Diesel averages €2.14 a litre across the EU. Qatari LNG supply is reduced after the strike on Ras Laffan, Russian LNG is due out of the EU market from January 2027, and Americans vote in the midterms on 3 November.

Four capitals are betting on the same calendar.

1. Russia and Ukraine are hitting each other’s energy systems, Moscow the Ukrainian grid near-daily since mid-July and Kyiv the Russian refineries, each trying to make the cold months unbearable for the other side’s population and its backers.

2. Europe pays for Kyiv’s war and for its own fuel at the same time.

3. US sells Europe the LNG and diesel it now depends on and controls the valve on Russian diesel through licences such as GL 135.

4. Tehran sets the risk premium in Hormuz, where a tanker was hit by a limpet mine on 30 October.

No player gains by de-escalating BEFORE the WINTER has tested the other side, so escalation through February 2027 is the rational choice for each, and the most likely path I see going forward.

The US election changes one variable. Before 3 November, the White House had every reason to HOLD fuel prices "down", and it issued a licence for Russian diesel after a call with Moscow to do it. 

BUT AFTER the vote that constraint loosens, and Washington’s tolerance for a harder line on Iran rises with it.

This is the SIGNAL, you want to understand from here onwards.

fujairah.t: The last time Iran used limpet mines against merchant shipping, I was the UK's regional maritime intelligence analyst at UKMCC in Bahrain. In May 2019, four sh…
fujairah.tx:
The last time Iran used limpet mines against merchant shipping, I was the UK's regional maritime intelligence analyst at UKMCC in Bahrain.

In May 2019, four ships were hit at anchor off Fujairah: the Saudi tankers AMJAD and AL MARZOQAH, the Norwegian tanker ANDREA VICTORY and the UAE bunker vessel A. MICHEL. A month later, KOKUKA COURAGEOUS and FRONT ALTAIR were attacked in the Gulf of Oman after their outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz.

On 29 October, it happened again. An Iranian small boat came alongside the outbound tanker LOUISE 1 north-east of Khasab and attached two limpet mines to her hull. The crew is safe, but the message is clear.

This is not a one-off. It is the latest step in a deliberate evolution of Iran's campaign at sea:

Geography. Attacks have spread from the Strait, which was the new norm, back into the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.

Tempo. From occasional strikes to several vessels a day.

Rhetoric. Iran repeatedly describes its attacks as sea mine strikes on ships using "unauthorised" routes. There is no evidence of sea mines. The narrative serves to deter traffic and blur responsibility.

Tactics. Multiple reports of UAVs striking or entering the ships' funnel, to cause maximum damage.

Weapon type. Missiles and drones, and now limpet mines placed by hand from small boats.

The last point matters most for the ships waiting to transit. A limpet mine can only be attached above the waterline while a ship is underway, but at anchor it can be placed below the waterline, often without the crew ever seeing the approach. That is exactly what we saw at Fujairah in 2019. A limpet mine below the waterline will cause significant damage and water ingress.

#MaritimeSecurity #StraitOfHormuz #LimpetMines #Shipping #MarineInsurance #RiskIntelligence

sevastopol.t: On this day in 1955, the flagship of the Soviet Black Sea Fleet blew up and rolled over in her own harbor in the dead of night, and hundreds of her sailors die…
sevastopol.tx:
On this day in 1955, the flagship of the Soviet Black Sea Fleet blew up and rolled over in her own harbor in the dead of night, and hundreds of her sailors died, many of them sealed alive inside the capsized hull while rescuers listened helplessly to them tapping on the steel. Seventy years later we still do not know for certain what killed her, and for decades the Soviet state pretended it had never happened. This is the Novorossiysk.

She had not been born Russian, and her earlier life was remarkable in itself. She began as the Giulio Cesare, an Italian battleship launched before the First World War and named for Julius Caesar. Rebuilt and modernized between the wars, she went to sea for Mussolini's navy in the Second World War and saw hard service. At the Battle of Calabria in 1940 she traded fire with the British Mediterranean Fleet and was struck by a shell from the battleship HMS Warspite at the staggering range of around fifteen miles, one of the longest range gunnery hits ever scored by one moving battleship on another. She was at anchor at Taranto the night the British torpedo bombers crippled the Italian fleet, and she survived that too. When Italy surrendered in 1943, she sailed into internment, her war over.

Then the victors divided the spoils. As part of Italy's war reparations, the old battleship was handed to the Soviet Union, and in 1949 she was renamed Novorossiysk and became the pride and flagship of the Soviet Black Sea Fleet at the great fortress port of Sevastopol. The Soviets refitted her and used her to train a new generation of sailors.

On the night of October 28 into the 29th, 1955, the Novorossiysk lay moored to a buoy in Sevastopol harbor, most of her crew asleep below. At around half past one in the morning, a tremendous explosion ripped through her from beneath the bow, forward of her first great gun turret. The blast tore a hole in her hull estimated at four by fourteen metres, punching clean up through the decks, the force consistent with over a thousand kilograms of high explosive, so large that investigators later suspected more than one charge had gone off. Hundreds of men were killed or maimed in that first instant.

What followed was a slow, agonizing catastrophe that should not have been fatal to the ship but became so. Water poured in through the enormous wound, and the efforts to save her went badly. Precious time was lost, decisions were muddled, and attempts to control the flooding and keep her in place rather than quickly running her aground in the shallows allowed the water to spread. Slowly the great battleship listed further and further over, and then, more than two hours after the explosion, she rolled completely over and capsized, turning turtle right there in the harbor in full view of the fleet.

And now came the worst of it. Hundreds of men were trapped alive inside the overturned hull, sealed into pockets of air in the flooded, upside down ship. Rescuers could hear them, the trapped sailors banging and tapping on the steel from within, calling for help that could not reach them in time. Divers and cutting teams worked frantically, and a handful of men were pulled out alive, some after days, but for most there was no escape. They died in the dark inside the hull of their own flagship. In all, around six hundred and seventeen men were lost, including sailors from other ships who had rushed over to help and died in the capsizing.

The cause has never been settled, and it remains one of the great mysteries of the Cold War at sea. The official Soviet finding, and the one most historians think likeliest, was that the Novorossiysk had set off a German magnetic mine left on the harbor bottom from the Second World War, perhaps dragged into contact by her own anchor chain as she moored. Searches of the seabed afterward turned up dozens of such old mines, some lying within a stone's throw of the blast. sevastopol.t: October 30, 1941. German forces close in on the great naval fortress of Sevastopol, in the Crimea, and begin one of the longest and most ferocious sieges of th…
sevastopol.tx:
October 30, 1941. German forces close in on the great naval fortress of Sevastopol, in the Crimea, and begin one of the longest and most ferocious sieges of the entire war. For eight months, the fortress city will hold out against everything the Germans can throw at it, and when it finally falls it will take some of the largest guns ever built to crack it.

This followed directly from the breakthrough at Perekop I told you about on the 27th. Once the Germans forced their way into the Crimea, they overran most of the peninsula quickly, but Sevastopol, in the southwest, was a different matter. It was the main base of the Soviet Black Sea Fleet, and it had been fortified over generations into one of the strongest fortress complexes in the world, ringed with concrete gun batteries, armored turrets, deep bunkers, trench lines, and minefields, built into the rugged coastal hills. The German 11th Army under Manstein, driving up to it in late October, found that they could not simply rush it, and around the 30th the siege settled in.

What followed was an epic of endurance. The Soviet defenders, soldiers, sailors, and marines of the Black Sea Fleet, along with the civilian population, dug in and held, through the autumn, through the winter, through the spring, resupplied and reinforced across the Black Sea by the Soviet navy, which ran ships into the besieged port under air attack to bring in men and ammunition and carry out the wounded. The Germans launched major assaults, pounded the fortress with artillery and bombing, and could not break in. Sevastopol held with a tenacity that became legendary, one of the Soviet Union's hero cities.

To finally take it, in the summer of 1942, the Germans assembled one of the most colossal concentrations of artillery in the history of war. They brought in enormous siege guns, including some of the largest ever built, giant railway guns firing shells of monstrous size, among them the vast gun nicknamed Dora, a weapon so huge it needed its own railway and a crew of hundreds, firing shells weighing several tons to smash the fortress's armored batteries and underground magazines. Under that apocalyptic bombardment and repeated ground assault, Sevastopol was at last battered into submission in July 1942, after eight months of siege, and fell to the Germans, who took the ruins and the surviving defenders.

The fall was a hard blow, but the defense had been magnificent, tying down a whole German army for months and inflicting heavy casualties. And the Soviets would be back. In 1944 they stormed the Crimea again and retook Sevastopol, this time breaking the German defenders in a matter of weeks, a mirror image of the long siege, as the tide of the war in the east had completely turned.

The siege that began at the end of October 1941 was one of the great fortress battles of the war, a city that held for eight months against overwhelming force and was finally cracked only by the largest guns ever made. Sevastopol's defense ranks with the epic sieges of history, and it began here, on the 30th, as Manstein's army closed in on the fortress by the sea.

sevastopol.t: October 27, 1941. In the far south of the Eastern Front, German forces smash through the narrow neck of land that is the only overland gateway to the Crimea, a…
sevastopol.tx:
October 27, 1941. In the far south of the Eastern Front, German forces smash through the narrow neck of land that is the only overland gateway to the Crimea, and pour into the peninsula. It opens one of the hardest-fought campaigns in the south, the conquest of the Crimea and the long, bloody siege of its great fortress city, Sevastopol.

The Crimea is a near-island, a large peninsula hanging into the Black Sea, connected to the mainland only by the narrowest of threads, the Perekop Isthmus, a strip of land just a few miles wide. That geography made it a natural fortress: an attacker had to force his way through the bottleneck of Perekop, across ground with no room to maneuver, straight into whatever defenses the enemy had built across the neck. The Soviets had fortified it, and the Crimea mattered enormously, both as a base from which Soviet aircraft could threaten the vital Romanian oil fields, and as the home of the Black Sea Fleet at Sevastopol.

The task of taking it fell to the German 11th Army, which came under the command of Erich von Manstein, one of the ablest German generals of the war. Through late October his troops battered their way through the Soviet defenses at Perekop in hard, costly fighting, forcing the narrow isthmus, and around the 27th they broke through into the open country of the peninsula beyond. Once through the bottleneck, the Germans fanned out and overran most of the Crimea with startling speed, driving the Soviet defenders before them, taking the peninsula in a matter of weeks.

But two things held out and turned the Crimean campaign into a long ordeal. One was the great naval fortress of Sevastopol, in the southwest, ringed with powerful fortifications, which the Germans could not take on the run. It held out under siege for months, through the winter and into the summer of 1942, one of the epic sieges of the war, defended ferociously and resupplied by the Soviet navy across the Black Sea, until Manstein finally reduced it in mid-1942 with a colossal concentration of artillery, including some of the largest guns ever built, and took it at enormous cost. The other was the Soviet determination to win the peninsula back, which led to huge amphibious landings and savage see-saw fighting around the Kerch Peninsula at the eastern end.

The breakthrough at Perekop on the 27th opened all of that, the overrunning of the Crimea, the terrible siege of Sevastopol, and the brutal battles for Kerch. And the Crimea, like everywhere the Germans conquered in the east, suffered the full horror of Nazi occupation behind the front, the murder of its Jews and the brutalization of its people. The campaign showcased Manstein's generalship, and it was one of the hardest-fought regional struggles of the whole Eastern Front, a peninsula taken and then held and then eventually lost again, all of it flowing from the forcing of that narrow neck of land at Perekop on this date.

30 October 1941. 85 years ago today.

At 4:35 PM, four old 102 mm guns of Coastal Battery No. 54 opened fire on a German column racing for Sevastopol. The siege had begun.

It lasted 247 days.

Manstein's 11th Army brought in the 80 cm "Dora" railway gun, the largest gun ever fired in war, and pounded the city with artillery and the Luftwaffe for weeks.

Sailors of the Black Sea Fleet came ashore and fought as infantry. That's them in the photo, charging through shell bursts in their caps and greatcoats.

On 1 July 1942 Admiral Oktyabrsky was flown out on Stavka's orders. General Petrov left by submarine that evening. Tens of thousands of men were left behind on Cape Chersonesus with nowhere to go.

Oktyabrsky reported:

"The remaining fighters are fighting heroically, they do not surrender, and when the situation is hopeless they destroy themselves... Sevastopol, as a city, no longer exists. It is destroyed."

Pockets on Cape Chersonesus kept fighting until 12 July.

sevastopol.t: Oct 29, 1914. A German admiral flying the Ottoman flag attacks Russia without a declaration of war. By the end of the week, the Ottoman Empire is in World War…
sevastopol.tx:
Oct 29, 1914. A German admiral flying the Ottoman flag attacks Russia without a declaration of war. By the end of the week, the Ottoman Empire is in World War I.

In August 1914, the German battlecruiser Goeben and light cruiser Breslau escaped British warships across the Mediterranean and ran into the Dardanelles.

The Ottoman Empire was officially neutral. So the Ottomans announced they had "bought" the two ships. Goeben became Yavuz Sultan Selim. Breslau became Midilli. Their German crews put on fezzes and stayed aboard.

Their commander, Rear Admiral Wilhelm Souchon, was made head of the entire Ottoman Navy.

Germany wanted the Ottomans in the war. So did the Ottoman war minister, Enver Pasha. But much of the Ottoman government didn't. Souchon and Enver decided to force the issue.

On Oct 27, the fleet left Constantinople, supposedly for maneuvers in the Black Sea.

Before dawn on Oct 29, it struck.

Ottoman torpedo boats crept into the harbor at Odessa and sank a Russian gunboat. At Sevastopol, home of the Russian Black Sea Fleet, Yavuz opened fire on the port. Russian coastal guns fired back and hit her. Other ships shelled Novorossiysk and Feodosia and laid mines along the coast. A Russian minelayer was sunk.

There had been no warning and no declaration of war.

Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire on Nov 2. Britain and France followed days later.

That one morning's raid opened new fronts in the Caucasus, Mesopotamia, Palestine and, the next year, at Gallipoli. Four years later, the Ottoman Empire no longer existed.

Breslau was sunk by mines in 1918. But the old Goeben served in the Turkish Navy for decades as Yavuz, and wasn't scrapped until the 1970s.

The last surviving dreadnought-era battlecruiser in the world was the ship that dragged an empire into war.

A special commission has preliminarily concluded that modernizing and restoring the heavy nuclear-powered missile cruiser Pyotr Velikiy would not be worthwhile, according to Vladimir Maltsev, chairman of the All-Russian Fleet Support Movement. He says the vessel is significantly worn out and is unlikely to return to active service. However, no final decision on its fate has been made.

Pyotr Velikiy is a Project 1144 Orlan-class heavy nuclear-powered missile cruiser. It is the largest combat surface warship in the world apart from aircraft carriers.

With a full displacement of 25,000 tonnes, it is equivalent in size to approximately two and a half American Ticonderoga-class cruisers. It is also the only nuclear-powered surface combatant of its kind, apart from heavy icebreakers.

Its armament is comparable to that of an entire squadron:

- 20 P-700 Granit anti-ship missiles.
- 96 Fort air-defence missiles.
- 128 Kinzhal surface-to-air missiles.
- 144 Kortik missile systems.

This is in addition to torpedo tubes, rocket launchers, a twin-barrel 130mm AK-130 naval gun and a Ka-27 anti-submarine helicopter housed in its hangar.

With adequate protection, a single Orlan-class cruiser can establish an air-denial zone over a substantial maritime area.

Pyotr Velikiy joined the Northern Fleet on April 18, 1998, nine years after being launched. From the beginning, it served as the fleet's flagship. Its mission was to operate within naval strike groups, provide air and anti-submarine defence for the formation, and threaten major enemy surface forces, particularly aircraft carrier groups.

However, the crew's baptism of fire did not come in a naval battle, but during a rescue operation.

In August 2000, the flagship led the search for the missing nuclear submarine Kursk and was the first to locate it using sonar. Pyotr Velikiy subsequently served as a command ship, coordinating the efforts of rescue teams.

Throughout the 2000s, Pyotr Velikiy frequently embarked on long-distance deployments, displaying the Russian Navy's St. Andrew's flag around the world.

Its most famous voyage took place between September 22, 2008, and March 10, 2009. The cruiser sailed from Severomorsk through the Mediterranean Sea, the Caribbean, the South Atlantic and the Indian Ocean.

In February, it took part in an anti-piracy operation in the Gulf of Aden and detained three Somali pirate vessels.

On September 12, 2012, Pyotr Velikiy embarked on its first Arctic deployment, leading a detachment of Northern Fleet warships and support vessels. During the expedition, it passed through the Vilkitsky Strait between the Taymyr Peninsula and Severnaya Zemlya.

From November 2013 to April 2014, the cruiser participated in an international operation to remove chemical weapons components from Syria.

From October 2016 to February 2017, Pyotr Velikiy provided protection for the Northern Fleet's carrier strike group in the eastern Mediterranean.

In every respect, it is an outstanding, powerful and exceptionally beautiful warship.

But 37 years since its launch is a very serious age for a naval vessel. There is no guarantee that shipbuilders will undertake the task of repairing the ageing giant.

However, its position as flagship may not remain vacant for long. By the end of the year, the heavy nuclear-powered missile cruiser Admiral Nakhimov is expected to join the Northern Fleet after an extensive modernization programme.

It has received new weapons, radars, communications and command systems, but remains an Orlan-class cruiser.

And as for Pyotr Velikiy, after its many years of service to the Motherland, it would make an excellent museum ship.

"In 2022, when trouble came to our homeland and our country found itself in a difficult situation, my friends and I decided to volunteer for the Special Military Operation (SMO).

We were all working in different fields, but we left our jobs behind and went to the front.

We served in the same unit. One of us never returned, another is still there, and I was wounded and discharged due to disability...

Not one of us has ever regretted that decision. We knew what we were there for, why we were there, and why we had to carry out that mission...

This is our Motherland. If not us, then who?"

— Andrey Fedoseev, SMO veteran and Deputy Chairman of the Council of Deputies of Severomorsk.

Recently, I visited the Russian Arctic, travelling to Severomorsk, Murmansk, Teriberka, and an authentic Sami village. You can watch our reports here, here, here, and here.

We are continuing our work, friends. More photos and videos will be coming soon.

We are gathering material for our "We Are Alive" project, delivering humanitarian aid, talking to people and listening to ordinary Russians whose lives have been affected by the war.

Watch, listen, subscribe, support, and get involved.

No one will help us except ourselves. We are all we have.

War correspondent Maryana Naumova

yongbyon.t: Mossad agents broke into a diplomat’s hotel room in Vienna, cloned his laptop in under an hour, and discovered dozens of color photos showing North Korean scie…
yongbyon.tx:
Mossad agents broke into a diplomat’s hotel room in Vienna, cloned his laptop in under an hour, and discovered dozens of color photos showing North Korean scientists inside an unmarked box-shaped building in the Syrian desert—triggering a stealth air raid that wiped out a covert plutonium reactor minutes before midnight.

The reason might surprise you.

In early 2007, Israeli intelligence was tracking suspicious cargo shipments between Pyongyang and Damascus. While Western agencies assumed Syria was merely modernizing ballistic missiles, Mossad Director Meir Dagan suspected something far more dangerous.

In March 2007, an operational window opened in Vienna:

Ibrahim Othman, head of the Syrian Atomic Energy Commission, arrived for an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) conference.

When Othman left his hotel for a dinner engagement, a specialized Mossad Kidon team breached his suite.

Operatives cloned his laptop's hard drive, planted Trojan spyware, and left the room completely undisturbed before his return.

When analysts back in Tel Aviv cracked the files, they were stunned:

The drive held dozens of high-resolution digital photographs taken inside a remote facility near Al-Kibar, in the Deir ez-Zor desert along the Euphrates River.

The images showed a gas-cooled, graphite-moderated nuclear reactor identical in design to North Korea's Yongbyon plutonium reactor.

Pictured side-by-side inside the facility were Chon Chiboo, a leading North Korean nuclear official, and senior Syrian engineers.

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert immediately dispatched Mossad and defense officials to Washington to brief President George W. Bush.

While US intelligence confirmed the facility was indeed a plutonium-production reactor built with North Korean assistance, Washington favored diplomatic pressure via the UN rather than kinetic military action.

Olmert refused to wait. Under the Begin Doctrine, an operational reactor in a hostile state could not be tolerated:

Once loaded with nuclear fuel rods, an airstrike would blanket the Euphrates Valley and downstream populations in lethal radioactive fallout. The countdown to strike was measured in months.

The mission was codenamed Operation Orchard (also referred to as Operation Outside the Box).

Before the airstrike, commandos from the elite Sayeret Matkal were covertly inserted by helicopter near Al-Kibar to collect soil samples, photograph perimeter defenses, and verify nuclear signatures.

On the night of September 5, 2007, the strike package took flight:

Four F-15I Ra'am fighters and four F-16I Sufa jets from the 69, 119, and 253 Squadrons departed Ramat David and Hatzerim airbases.

Instead of flying east over Jordan, the aircraft headed west over the Mediterranean, climbed north, and banked east along the Turkish-Syrian border.

Israel's electronic warfare and cyber units deployed an airborne algorithmic weapon codenamed Suter: they hacked and fed false-sky data directly into Syria’s modern Russian-built radar network. The screens showed tranquil, empty airspace while eight strike fighters roared beneath radar shadows.

Shortly after 11:30 PM, the strike package dropped down onto Al-Kibar:

Diving out of the dark sky, the jets unleashed 17 tons of precision-guided ordnance, including AGM-65 Maverick missiles and 500-pound laser-guided penetration bombs.

The cubic concrete containment building was completely flattened, collapsing into its subterranean foundations in seconds.

At 12:01 AM on September 6, the mission commander radioed the prearranged Hebrew code word back to the subterranean command bunker in Tel Aviv: "Arizona." All eight Israeli aircraft returned to base completely undamaged.

What followed was one of the most remarkable diplomatic silences in modern warfare:

Neither Israel nor Syria acknowledged what had occurred. Prime Minister Olmert imposed a strict military gag order on Israeli press, preventing Syrian President Bashar al-Assad from facing public pressure to retal

yongbyon.t: South Korea's spy chief has confirmed it: one remark by Unification Minister Chung Dong-young led the U.S. to restrict intelligence sharing on North Korea. In…
yongbyon.tx:
South Korea's spy chief has confirmed it: one remark by Unification Minister Chung Dong-young led the U.S. to restrict intelligence sharing on North Korea.

In March, Minister Chung told lawmakers North Korea enriches uranium at Yongbyon, Kangson and Kusong. Seoul had only ever confirmed the first two. By early April, Washington began limiting what it shared.

On Thursday, NIS Director Lee Jong-seok told the Intelligence Committee the Kusong remark triggered the curbs. He called them limited and said Korea's own reconnaissance assets can fill the gap. Minister Chung says he only repeated what U.S. think tanks had already published.

The curbs have now lasted seven months. In June, Washington asked that Korea's spy agency be kept out of a U.S.-Korea-Japan meeting on North Korean cyber threats.
Allies share secrets only when they trust each other to keep them.

Should a minister whose words cost the alliance seven months of intelligence keep his job?

Source: Kookmin Ilbo, NK News, Korea Times, UPI
